queue.dek: Genocide is the crime of crimes, and it requires a heightened level of proof. In its Myanmar ruling, the ICJ abandoned that standard, writes Roy K. Altman.
queue.opening: Yesterday’s long-awaited ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ)—finding Myanmar guilty of genocide in a case brought by the Republic of The Gambia—may have imperiled the court’s own legitimacy. Along the way, the ICJ—the branch of the United Nations’ judicial system that adjudicates disputes between states—has violated some foundational precepts of our Western tradition in ways that may expose any government, including our own, to arbitrary genocide prosecutions in the future. The ICJ’s finding was long awaited not because anyone had shown much interest over the last 10 years in Myanmar’s brutal campaign against its minority Muslim population, known as the Rohingya, in a war that started in 2016. The outsize attention has had little to do with either Myanmar or The Gambia and a great deal to do with the watered-down definition of genocide the court was being asked to adopt.
